links.note: 451 says greatness fears small company (சிற்றினம் அஞ்சும் பெருமை) while smallness takes it for kin. 201 says those given to evil deeds do not fear them but the excellent do (தீவினையார் அஞ்சார் விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்). In both, what marks the better person is fear of the thing the worse person is at ease with, once about company and once about deeds.

451 says smallness at once surrounds itself with small company as kin (சுற்றமாச் சூழ்ந்து விடும்). 976 says the aim of cherishing the great and taking them on (பெரியாரைப் பேணிக் கொள்வேம் என்னும் நோக்கு) is absent from the minds of the small. Together they give both halves: the small are drawn to their like and have no wish to seek their betters.

452 uses water changing with the nature of the land it meets (நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர் திரிந்து) for understanding taking on the nature of one's company. In 1323 a lover calls the pair those joined as water with earth (நிலத்தொடு நீர் இயைந்தன்னார்), and Parimelazhagar explains that image by water taking on the land's nature. The same picture of water absorbed into soil is a caution about company in one place and a figure of union in the other.

452 says water takes the nature of the land, and understanding the nature of one's company (இனத்தியல்பு). 959 says the sprout shows what lay in the ground (நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை கால் காட்டும்) and speech shows the family one was born in. Both treat a person as carrying the mark of the ground they stand in, 452 for the company kept and 959 for birth.

453 says perception comes from the mind, but the word that one is 'such a person' comes from one's company (இன்னான் எனப்படும் சொல் இனத்தான் ஆம்). 505 says the touchstone of greatness and smallness is each person's own deeds (தத்தம் கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as that and nothing else. If 453 is read as saying what a person really is, and not only what people call them, the two name different tests of character: company or deeds.

454 says understanding only appears to be in the mind and really lies in one's company (மனத்துளது போலக் காட்டி ... இனத்துளதாகும்). 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, one's own real understanding prevails (தன் உண்மை அறிவே மிகும்). On the reading of உண்மை அறிவு as native intelligence (Subramuniyaswami and Kalaignar; Parimelazhagar makes it the understanding fate has given), 373 holds understanding to be fixed within the person, while 454 places its source outside, in the company kept.

34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்து அறன்). 455 says purity of mind and purity of deed both come leaning on purity of company (இனந்தூய்மை தூவா வரும்). Read together, the inner purity that 34 makes sufficient is itself dependent, in 455, on something outside the person.

298 says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truthfulness (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). 455 says purity of mind comes resting on purity of company. The book thus gives inner purity two supports, one's own truthfulness and the people one keeps.

456 says the pure of mind have a good எச்சம் (எச்சம் நன்றாகும்), and 114 says whether people were just or not is seen by their எச்சம் (எச்சத்தாற் காணப்படும்). Parimelazhagar takes the word as offspring in both; Kalaignar takes it in both as what remains after one, good name or blame. Either way both verses make what a person leaves behind the evidence of the inner quality.

456 says no deed fails to turn out well for those whose company is pure (இனந்தூயார்க்கு இல்லை நன்றாகா வினை), and Parimelazhagar gives the reason: their deeds are thought through with good company. 462 states that mechanism directly: nothing is hard to attain for those who act after examining the matter with chosen company (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி).

457 says goodness of mind gives gain (ஆக்கம்) and goodness of company gives all praise as well (இனநலம் எல்லாப் புகழும் தரும்). 651 has the same two-step form but says goodness of companions gives gain and goodness of action gives all that is wanted (துணைநலம் ஆக்கம் தரூஉம் வினைநலம் வேண்டிய எல்லாம் தரும்); Parimelazhagar there reads companions as giving wealth only. Company holds the higher place in 457 and the lower in 651, where one's own action outranks it.

458 says that even for the worthy who have goodness of mind in full, goodness of company is a safeguard (ஏமாப்பு உடைத்து). 448 says a king without the guard of people who rebuke him (இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத ஏமரா மன்னன்) perishes even with no one to ruin him. Both use the same word for protection (ஏமம்), and 448 shows what the company protects against: one's own unchecked faults.

243 says those whose hearts are joined to அருள் do not enter the dark world of pain (அருள் சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சினார்க்கு இல்லை இருள் சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம் புகல்). 459 agrees that the next world comes from goodness of mind (மனநலத்தின் ஆகும் மறுமை) and adds that even this is made secure by goodness of company. The afterlife that 243 rests on the heart alone is given a second support in 459.

460 says there is no support greater than good company and nothing that afflicts more than bad company (தீயினத்தின் அல்லற் படுப்பதூஉம் இல்). 450 says letting go the tie with the good is ten times worse than taking on the enmity of many (பல்லார் பகை கொளலிற் பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்து). 460 names keeping bad company as the worst harm and 450 names losing good company; both rank these above open enemies, and Parimelazhagar glosses 460's second half as enmity.

460 is built on the form 'nothing beyond X as support, nothing beyond Y as affliction' (நல்லினத்தின் ஊங்கும் துணையில்லை). 32 uses the same form and the same word ஊங்கு for virtue: no gain beyond virtue, no ruin beyond forgetting it (அறத்தினூஉங்கு ஆக்கமும் இல்லை). The pairing shows good company being given, in the book on statecraft, the kind of unqualified ranking the opening chapters give to virtue.

461 tells one to weigh what will be lost, what will be gained and the later yield, and then act (அழிவதூஉம் ஆவதூஉம் ... ஊதியமும் சூழ்ந்து செயல்). 676 has the same closing command and also three items, but different ones: what it takes to finish, the obstacles, and the great yield at completion (முடிவும் இடையூறும் ... படுபயனும் பார்த்துச் செயல்). 461 is an account of cost and return; 676 keeps the return and adds the course of the work itself.

461 lists the outcomes to be weighed before acting: loss, gain and later yield. 471, opening the next chapter with the same imperative, lists the strengths to be weighed: of the deed, oneself, the opponent and the allies (வினைவலியும் தன்வலியும் மாற்றான் வலியும் துணைவலியும் தூக்கிச் செயல்). The second supplies what the first's calculation of gain and loss depends on.

462 says nothing is hard to attain for those who act after examining a matter with chosen company and thinking it through themselves (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி). 568 gives the negative case: the fortune of a king who does not think matters through with his circle (இனத்தாற்றி எண்ணாத வேந்தன்) and then rages will shrink. Both make deliberation with one's இனம் the condition of success, stated once as promise and once as warning.

462 speaks of deliberating with a company that has been chosen (தெரிந்த இனம்). 445 says that since those who deliberate for him serve as his eyes, a king must take his counsellors only after deliberation (சூழ்வாரைச் சூழ்ந்து கொளல்). 445 supplies the earlier step that 462's word தெரிந்த assumes: the advisers themselves have to be examined first.

463 says those with understanding do not take up a venture that loses the capital for the sake of gain (ஆக்கம் கருதி முதல் இழக்கும் செய்வினை). 449 says those without capital have no profit (முதலிலார்க்கு ஊதியம் இல்லை), using it as a likeness for a ruler without support. Both use the merchant's முதல், and 449 gives the reason behind 463: profit comes only from capital, so risking the capital for profit defeats itself.

463 says the wise do not undertake what loses the principal in hope of gain. 932 asks whether gamblers, who get one and lose a hundred (ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும் சூதர்), have any way of living well. The gambler is the plain case of the venture 463 rules out, a small gain pursued at the cost of what one already had.

464 says those who fear the harm called disgrace do not begin what is not clear to them (தெளிவிலதனைத் தொடங்கார் ... அஞ்சுபவர்). 172 has the same form: those ashamed of unfairness do not do blameworthy things out of desire for the gain (பழிப்படுவ செய்யார் நடுவன்மை நாணுபவர்). In both a fear or shame is what holds a person back, in 172 from a wrong act and in 464 from an unexamined one.

428 says not fearing what should be feared is folly and fearing it is the work of the knowing (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில்). 464 gives one such fear and what it does: fear of disgrace (இளிவென்னும் ஏதப்பாடு) keeps people from beginning what they have not made clear. The general rule of 428 is applied in 464 to the start of an undertaking.

465 says setting out without thinking through every aspect is a way of setting one's enemies in a planting bed (பகைவரைப் பாத்திப் படுப்பது); Parimelazhagar reads this as establishing them in ground where they grow. 718 says speaking before those who understand is like pouring water into the bed of a growing plant (வளர்வதன் பாத்தியுள் நீர் சொரிந்தற்று). The same garden bed stands for fostering growth in both, wanted in 718 and brought on oneself in 465.

465 says rising without full deliberation (வகையறச் சூழாது எழுதல்) benefits the enemy. 473 says many who did not know their own strength pressed on in enthusiasm and broke midway (ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் பலர்). 473 names one of the things left unconsidered, one's own strength, and shows the cost to oneself where 465 shows the gain to the enemy.

465 pictures a rash attack as planting the enemy in a bed where he will grow. 879, in a chapter on enemies, says to cut a thorn tree while it is young, since when hardened it wounds the hand that cuts it (இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க). Both treat the enemy as a plant whose growth is the danger: 879 says to stop it early, 465 warns against tending it by one's own haste.

466 says one is ruined by doing what is not fit to do, and also by not doing what is fit (செய்தக்க செய்யாமை யானும் கெடும்). 510 says trusting someone unexamined and doubting someone already examined and trusted both bring unending trouble (தேரான் தெளிவும் தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்). Each verse sets an error of excess beside an error of defect and gives them the same result, once for action and once for trust.

466 says both doing the unfit and leaving the fit undone bring ruin. 672 gives the same two-sided rule for timing: delay what should be done slowly, and do not delay what must be done without delay (தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால தூங்கற்க தூங்காது செய்யும் வினை). 672 carries 466's point, that holding back is no safer than acting, into the question of when to act.

467 says to think and then resolve on a task, and that saying 'we will think after resolving' is a fault (எண்ணித் துணிக ... துணிந்தபின் எண்ணுவம் என்பது இழுக்கு). 671 says deliberation ends in reaching resolve, and it is bad for that resolve to rest in delay (அத்துணிவு தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). 467 guards the step before துணிவு and 671 the step after it: thought first, then no lingering.

467 fixes the order for action: think first, then resolve, and no thinking postponed until after. 509 fixes the same order for trusting people: trust no one without examining, and after examining, trust what is to be trusted (தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக). In both the examination belongs wholly before the commitment, and the commitment is then not to be reopened.

467 requires deliberation before any undertaking. 1024 says that for those who labour for their family without delay, the work reaches its end by itself without deliberation (சூழாமல் தானே முடிவெய்தும்); Parimelazhagar reads this as their not needing to work out the means. Taken at its word, 1024 names a case where prompt effort stands in for the forethought 467 demands.

616 says effort produces fortune and lack of effort brings want (முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும்). 468 says exertion that is not made by the right way (ஆற்றின் வருந்தா வருத்தம்) will give way even if many stand guarding it. 468 puts a condition on 616's praise of effort: it has to follow the proper method, and neither strain nor helpers make up for that.

468 says effort without the right method fails whatever support it has (பலர் நின்று போற்றினும் பொத்துப்படும்). 640 says those without practical capacity leave things unfinished even after planning them in proper order (முறைப்படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவிலவே செய்வர் திறப்பாடு இலாதவர்). The two are complementary failures: effort without method in 468, and method on paper without the ability to carry it out in 640.

469 says there is error even in doing good when it is done without knowing each person's character (அவரவர் பண்பறிந்து ஆற்றாக்கடை). 1078 says the worthy are of use at a word, while the base, like sugar-cane, are of use only when crushed (சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர் சான்றோர் கரும்புபோல் கொல்லப் பயன்படும் கீழ்). 1078 is an instance of the difference in character 469 says must be known first: the approach that works on one kind of person does nothing with another.

469 says doing good can itself be a mistake if the character of the person is not taken into account. 987 asks what worth has achieved if it does not do what is sweet even to those who have done one harm (இன்னா செய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்), which makes the recipient's conduct irrelevant. The conflict holds if 469's நன்றாற்றல் is read as doing good in general, as Pope and Kalaignar take it; Parimelazhagar narrows it to a king's use of gifts and soft words toward other kings, and on that reading the two do not meet.

470 says to think and do what will not be scorned, because the world does not accept what does not accord with oneself (கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது உலகு). 140 says those who have not learned to conduct themselves in accord with the world lack understanding, however much they have studied (உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்). Both make the world's acceptance a test that sound judgement has to meet, 470 for a ruler's choice of action and 140 for conduct in general.

470 tells the one who acts to avoid what the world will scorn and not accept. 280 tells the ascetic that neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if he gives up what the world has condemned (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின்); Parimelazhagar takes 'the world' there as the high-minded. The same measure, what the world rejects, governs a king's policy in one verse and a renouncer's conduct in the other.
